stem: A hospital is designing a transition-of-care program for clients discharged after a heart-failure hospitalization. Which program component best aligns with the AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline?

options.A: Provide clear discharge instructions on medications, weight and symptom monitoring, arrange timely follow-up, and communicate the transition plan to outpatient clinicians.
options.B: Limit discharge education to the medication list because weight monitoring and symptom-response plans are best deferred to a later outpatient visit.
options.C: Avoid early follow-up after discharge because contacting clients soon after hospitalization has no role in continuity of heart-failure care.
options.D: Use the program as a replacement for ongoing outpatient heart-failure management once the client has received discharge instructions.

rationale: The AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline recommends comprehensive transitional planning after heart-failure hospitalization. Discharge material should address medications, follow-up, weight monitoring, and what to do if symptoms worsen, and the transition plan should be communicated clearly to clinicians providing follow-up care. The guideline also identifies early outpatient follow-up as a central element of transitional care. Therefore, A is correct. B omits key discharge content, C rejects an emphasized continuity strategy, and D incorrectly substitutes a transition program for ongoing care.
educational_objective: Plan heart-failure transitions of care using comprehensive discharge education, symptom/weight monitoring instructions, timely follow-up, and clear communication with outpatient clinicians.
source_organization: American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/Heart Failure Society of America
source_document_title: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
source_locator: Hospitalized HF → transitions/discharge supportive text: written discharge instructions should address activity, diet, discharge medications, follow-up appointment, weight monitoring, cardiac rehabilitation, and what to do if symptoms worsen; the transitional plan and medication/diagnosis changes should be communicated to outpatient clinicians. Early outpatient follow-up is described as a central element of transitional care and may reduce gaps in understanding; disease-management/case-management programs may decrease rehospitalization.
source_claim_supported: Directly supports comprehensive discharge education, early follow-up, and communication of the transition plan as evidence-based heart-failure continuity-of-care strategies.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care → Case Management/Continuity of Care: provide discharge education, coordinate care across settings, facilitate referrals/follow-up, and communicate client information needed for continuity of care.
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — transition planning and continuity after heart-failure hospitalization
correction_summary: Reclassified the item from Safety/Infection Prevention and Control to Management of Care and replaced the vague claim that programs simply reduce 'preventable readmissions' by addressing named causes. The final item tests the specific transition components directly described in the primary heart-failure guideline without attributing every readmission to nonadherence or delayed symptom recognition.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Heart-failure transition of care and readmission-risk reduction
audit_findings.source_authority: Primary AHA/ACC/HFSA heart-failure clinical practice guideline.
audit_findings.currentness: The 2022 HF guideline remains the current dedicated clinical practice guideline for heart-failure management at the audit date.

claim_by_claim.stem: A post-hospitalization transition program is explicitly addressed in the current HF guideline.
claim_by_claim.A: Correct because all listed elements are directly described in discharge/transitional-care supportive text.
claim_by_claim.B: Incorrect because discharge education should include weight monitoring, follow-up, and what to do when symptoms worsen, not medication information alone.
claim_by_claim.C: Incorrect because early outpatient follow-up is described as a central element of transitional care.
claim_by_claim.D: Incorrect because transition planning supports continuity and does not replace ongoing outpatient HF management.
claim_by_claim.rationale: Avoids claiming a guaranteed readmission reduction or assigning specific causal proportions to nonadherence/diet/symptom delay.
claim_by_claim.educational_objective: Specific to multidisciplinary transition planning after HF hospitalization.

audit_findings.distractor_audit: B tests incomplete discharge teaching, C rejects early continuity, and D confuses transition support with replacement of longitudinal care. Each is realistic and distinct.
audit_findings.ambiguity_and_second_answer: Only A contains the guideline-supported set of transition components. No other option is partially equivalent.
audit_findings.cueing: All options describe program design decisions rather than isolated facts; the key requires continuity-of-care knowledge.
audit_findings.blueprint: Management of Care is a stronger fit than Safety because the construct is discharge planning, care coordination, follow-up, and communication across settings.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited whether early follow-up is a mandatory fixed interval and whether the program can be said to prevent readmission. The final item uses 'timely follow-up' and guideline transition components without a universal interval or guaranteed outcome. No unresolved conflict remains.
